title: Challenge is wages, not jobs. Expanding Jan Vishwas interventions can help
where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Manish Sabharwal, Teamlease Services)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Growth and development · GS2 › Government policies; Transparency and accountability; Citizen-centric governance · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: After decriminalising thousands of offences, the writer argues the next Jan Vishwas phase should make every rule published, knowable and trust-based, because India's problem is low wages, not a lack of jobs.
ideas: Wages, not jobs: India's problem is job quality, not quantity; a third of the workforce is in employed poverty, trapped in informal wage work and self-employment.
GS3 · Employment
India's employment challenge is low-wage informality, not joblessness; the fix lies in formal, high-wage job creation.
Regulatory cholesterol: China's per-capita GDP is five times India's (on par in 1991), not because of effort but because of India's lack of transparency, consistency and trust in law enforcement.
GS3 · Growth / GS2 · Governance
Regulatory cholesterol, not lack of talent or effort, explains much of India's per-capita income gap with China.

Six toxic thought worlds: prior approval (prohibited till permitted), enforcing the unenforceable, process as punishment, blindness to 25+ instruments below Acts, laws for edge cases, and excessive criminalisation.
GS2 · Administrative reform
India's regulatory mindset (prior approval, process as punishment, over-criminalisation) treats the citizen as a suspect.

Three next steps: Siddhant (trust-based regulation on freedom, necessity, proportionality, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants), Sangreh (a single legal record as DPI) and Ashwasan (only published obligations are enforceable).
GS2 · Citizen-centric governance
Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to trust, knowability and certainty through Siddhant, Sangreh and Ashwasan.

Law must be knowable: ignorance of law is no excuse only if the State makes law accessible; earlier attempts failed on design, capacity, fragmented power, attention and technology, and lacked a binding duty to publish.
GS2 · Rule of law / Transparency
A citizen's duty to obey the law presupposes the State's duty to publish it; unpublished rules breed uncertainty and corruption.
keywords: Accumulated rules, filings and permissions that clog enterprise
Regulatory cholesterol raises the cost of formality and pushes firms into informality.
Employed poverty shows India's real problem is wage quality, not job quantity.
A prohibited-till-permitted regime presumes guilt and slows enterprise.
The procedure itself harasses the innocent
When process is punishment, even compliant citizens bear the cost of regulation.
Ignorance of the law is no excuse
Ignorantia juris holds only when the State makes the law knowable.
One machine-readable source for every legal obligation (Sangreh)
A legal DPI like Sangreh can do for compliance what UPI did for payments.
examples: Supreme Court on knowable law
Harla v State of Rajasthan (1952) rejected secret laws; B K Srinivasan (1987) moved to knowability; Viraj Impex (2019) held law operative only when published
GS2 · Judiciary / Rule of law
From Harla (1952) to Viraj Impex (2019), courts have held unpublished law cannot bind citizens.
Global single-source registers
US Federal Register, UK legislation.gov.uk, EU EUR-Lex, Singapore Statutes Online
GS2 · Comparative governance
Democracies like the US, UK and Singapore publish all binding rules in one register; India's Sangreh can follow.
Transparency of Rules Act (TORA)
Sanjeev Sanyal's draft: every enforceable obligation must be published on Sangreh
GS4
GS2 · Transparency / GS4 · Probity
TORA would make publication a precondition for enforcement, curbing discretion and corruption.
Adam Smith and the Constitution
250 years of The Wealth of Nations, 76 of the Constitution: both see government as expanding freedom
GS2 · Constitutional values / Essay
Both Adam Smith and the Constitution see the State as an enabler of freedom, not its gatekeeper.
pyqs: Trust through rule of law: Sangreh and Ashwasan are trust tools.
Job-rich, productive growth: formal high-wage jobs through deregulation.
Informalisation: regulatory cholesterol as a cause.
Civil servant as enabler: Siddhant's adoption by civil servants.

trend.t: Governance questions moved from regulatory autonomy (2015) to the e-governance interactive model (2024) and trust built through rule of law and participation (2026). Employment moved from informalisation (2016) to job-rich, productive growth (2022). GS4 (2025) asks the civil servant to be an enabler, not a regulator.
trend.watch: 'Trust' is the new keyword in GS2 and GS4. Prepare trust-based, citizen-centric governance with examples such as Jan Vishwas, GST arrest powers and self-certification.
focus: Rule of law: knowability of law

potential: "India's challenge is not jobs but wages." Examine, and suggest reforms to promote formal, high-wage employment. (15 marks)
Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed? (10 marks)
"The citizen's duty to know the law presupposes the State's duty to make it knowable." Comment. (10 marks)

practice.q: Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed?

answer.t: Jan Vishwas has decriminalised thousands of offences, yet a third of India's workforce remains in employed poverty, held back by regulatory cholesterol.

pts.t: The State treats citizens and firms as honest stakeholders, not suspects.
Fewer jail terms for minor lapses reduce the fear of becoming formal.
Less 'process is punishment' lets firms combine land, labour and capital.
Less discretion means fewer chances for rent-seeking.
It attacks the root of informality.
Freedom, necessity and proportionality to guide regulation, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants.
One machine-readable legal DPI, unifying gazettes and India Code.
Only published obligations should be enforceable.
Periodic pruning of circulars and rules.

answer.t: Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to certainty, so that what is wrong with India's regulation is fixed by what is right with its democracy.

title: How welfare board will function, what changes for unorganised, gig workers
where: Economy, page 10 (Ravi Dutta Mishra & Aanchal Magazine)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Labour reforms · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections; Statutory bodies
summary: Follow-up: the Labour Ministry has notified two social security boards (40 members for unorganised workers, 22 for gig and platform workers) under the Code on Social Security.
evolution: Labour Ministry notifies the National Social Security Board under the Code on Social Security (Economy, page 23).
Details: two boards, aggregator contributions to a social security fund, and EPFO coverage widened.
ideas: Two boards, not one: a 40-member board for unorganised workers and a 22-member board for gig and platform workers, which includes aggregators such as quick-commerce and delivery platforms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
Separate boards recognise that gig and platform workers need schemes designed for platform work.
Who pays: aggregators must contribute 1–2% of annual turnover to a social security fund, capped at 5% of what they pay workers; the fund also draws on governments, CSR and fines.
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregator contributions put part of the cost of gig workers' security on the platforms that profit from them.
What it covers: schemes for life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and crèches.
GS2 · Welfare
Social security for gig workers spans life-cycle risks, from maternity to old age.
Wider formal coverage: EPFO provisions now apply to all establishments with 20 or more employees, regardless of industry, not only those in the old schedule.
GS3 · Labour reforms
Extending EPFO to all establishments with 20+ workers widens formal social security.
keywords: Pooled fund for unorganised, gig and platform workers
A dedicated Social Security Fund gives gig workers' schemes a stable financing base.
Platforms paying a share of turnover towards workers' welfare
The aggregator levy shares the cost of social protection with platforms.
data: Aggregators' contribution to the social security fund, capped at 5% of amounts payable to workers
Code on Social Security, via IE
Aggregators must contribute 1–2% of turnover to gig workers' social security, capped at 5% of payouts (Code on Social Security).
examples: Aggregators on the gig workers' board
Platforms sit with worker bodies to design welfare schemes
GS2 · Tripartism, statutory bodies · GS3 · Digital economy
Putting aggregators and worker bodies on one board shows tripartism adapting to the platform economy.
pyqs: The gig economy and women's empowerment.
